extracted.intended_audience: students, journalists, political scientists, policymakers, and general readers interested in media and public opinion
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and criteria for analyzing how public opinion is formed, communicated, and acted upon—especially the roles of mental images, newspapers, stereotypes, interests, organized intelligence, and the limits of reason in politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictures in our heads / pseudo-environment
rubrics_metrics.description: The insertion between man and his environment of a pseudo-environment: people act on their mental images of the world rather than on the world itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the degree to which individuals' or groups' behavior is guided by simplified, imagined 'pictures' rather than direct acquaintance with facts. Use examples (islanders, wartime misconceptions, individual hallucination) to test how actions derive from mental images; identify when a 'pseudo-environment' risks maladjustment because consequences unfold in the real environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maps and schematic models as necessary simplifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the real environment is 'altogether too big, too complex, and too fleeting', people reconstruct it on simpler models or 'maps' to act effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the map/model used is appropriate to the actor's needs and whether its degree of fidelity is acknowledged. Distinguish legitimate schematic simplifications (useful models) from misleading distortions that insert biased coastlines or omit crucial facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangular relationship: scene, picture, response
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysts must recognize the triangular relationship among the scene of action (real world), the human picture of that scene (mental model), and the human response to that picture working out upon the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating decisions or political behavior, trace (1) the objective situation, (2) the mental picture people held of it, and (3) how responses enacted against that picture affected the real situation. Use this triangle to explain apparent misfits between intentions and outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness, time-differential, and attention limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The rate at which reason or accurate information can develop is often slower than the rate at which political action must be taken; time and attention are scarce resources for news and public reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge proposals and reporting against their relevant time-horizon: is data current enough for the decision? Evaluate whether urgency pushes actors to decisive but underinformed acts, and whether longer-term reasoning was feasible or ignored. Consider 'time-differential' when assessing plans' practicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotypes: formation, defense, blind spots, and detection
rubrics_metrics.description: Stereotypes are simplified, persistent pictures that organize perception and behavior; they function as defenses but create blind spots and errors of judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify prevalent stereotypes in discourse; inspect how they simplify complex realities, defend identities, and produce systematic errors. Use tools for detection (contrast with facts, look for resistance to disconfirming evidence) and evaluate the costs/uses of stereotypes in mobilizing opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interests and the enlistment/transfer of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Public opinion is shaped by interests—how interests are enlisted, transferred, or aggregated affects the making of a 'common will'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze who benefits from a particular framing, whether appeals successfully recruit or shift interests, and how leaders or institutions mediate transfer of interest between elites and masses. Evaluate the authenticity of 'common will' vs manufactured consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic personalities and the manufacture of heroes/devils
rubrics_metrics.description: Public opinion often concentrates on symbolic persons who are cast as heroes or devils; these symbols can unify or polarize and simplify complex causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how personalities are constructed by media and publics, how symbolic status substitutes for fuller explanation, and the behavioral effects (hero-worship, scapegoating). Check for staged attributes (e.g., props, visual cues) that create symbolic authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness and the nature of news
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature of news is tied to what can be pictured and what arouses feeling in those who did not experience the event; news operates by supplying images that substitute for direct experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate items for their capacity to form clear, credible images in readers' minds; test whether reporting supplies necessary context to convert remote events into comprehensible impressions and whether it distinguishes image from verified fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspapers as businesses: the buying public and reader relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers operate within a market ('the buying public'); their content is shaped by time, attention, commercial pressures, and readers' expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating journalistic outputs, account for market incentives (advertising, circulation), editorial choices about attention allocation, and the constraints these place on depth, accuracy, and independence. Distinguish between business-driven distortions and editorial conscience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth, editorial conscience, and journalistic ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: News should aspire to truth and a conscience: distinguishing truth from rumor and deceptive pseudo-facts is essential for healthy public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess sourcing, verification practices, transparency about uncertainty, and resistance to concealed payments or partisan manipulation. Use examples (Senate reaction to rumor) to gauge failures and the institutional remedies (inquiry, official reporting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Organized intelligence and the role of specialized information work
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective public opinion and policy depend on organized intelligence—institutions that collect, analyze, and supply reliable information to decision-makers and the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether intelligence is institutionalized, independent, timely, and integrated into decision processes. Look for 'entering wedge' opportunities where better intelligence can improve public understanding; judge credibility, methods, and institutional protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of appeal to reason in politics
rubrics_metrics.description: Reason has limited immediate effectiveness in politics because actors lack shared premises, expertise cannot be quickly disseminated, and emergency action often requires rhetoric or force rather than deliberation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing reason-based policies or communication, judge feasibility given time constraints, audience receptivity, and extent to which reasoned arguments can be translated into accessible images or incentives. Prefer long-run institutional and educational strategies where immediate reasoned persuasion is impractical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of rhetoric, symbols, and expedients in crises
rubrics_metrics.description: In urgent political situations, appeals to emotion, slogans, symbols, or force may be the only practicable means to restore order or act swiftly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate crisis communications for effectiveness and ethical limits: were expedients proportionate, were longer-term reasoned remedies preserved, and was there later accountability to reintroduce deliberation?

rubrics_metrics.name: Seven sins against public opinion (normative constraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hatred, intolerance, suspicion, bigotry, secrecy, fear, and lying are corrosive to the appeal to reason and poison public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this normative checklist to condemn and avoid manipulative practices in building public support. When assessing rhetoric or policy, flag instances of these seven elements and prioritize transparency, tolerance, and truthfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting and correcting rumors and pseudo-facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Rumors, deliberate lies, and pseudo-facts can rapidly alter public pictures and provoke action; institutional checks (investigations, official reports) are necessary to correct them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate mechanisms for verification within media and political bodies; examine how quickly and effectively corrections are issued and whether partisan needs inhibited inquiry (e.g., Senators treating rumor as fact).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fictions vs useful schemata: degree of fidelity and disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Fictions (simplifications, models, stylizations) vary in fidelity; a fiction is not misleading if its degree of fidelity is understood and taken into account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using analogies, models, or narrative simplifications, disclose their limits and intended scope. Assess whether the audience is warned about simplifications or misled into treating them as full reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention economy: speed, words, and format constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Attention, speed of reporting, and the chosen words/format shape what is communicated and how it is understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether constraints of speed and limited attention led to loss of nuance or encouraged sensationalism. Recommend format choices (depth pieces, follow-ups) when complexity requires it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion as aggregate of many partial symbolic pictures
rubrics_metrics.description: In normal times, public opinion is composed of many partial symbols and competing pictures, subject to checks, comparisons, and argument, rather than a single monolithic image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze plurality and heterogeneity in opinions, look for balancing forces (classes, parties, interest groups), and avoid overgeneralizing from dramatic examples; measure stability and fragility of symbolic coalitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of institutions and organizations in mediating opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions (parties, corporations, voluntary associations, presses) mediate between private pictures and public decisions; their structures and incentives influence outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate institutional design: representation, accountability, incentives, and capacity to gather and distribute accurate information. Assess how institutional fragmentation or concentration affects the quality of public opinion.
